deep.reconstruction:
The page holds four unrelated notes. The page cites the SS 1902 lecture notes, so it was written after 1902.

(1) When is cos(2π/n) rational? Suppose cos(2π/n) = α ∈ Q. Put ζ = e^{2πi/n} = cos(2π/n) + i sin(2π/n). ζ is a root of x^n − 1, so it is an algebraic integer ('ganze Zahl' here means ganze algebraische Zahl). Then ζ^{-1} = ζ^{n−1} is also an algebraic integer, so ζ + ζ^{-1} = 2α is one too. A rational algebraic integer is a rational integer ('ganze rationale Zahl'). Hence 2α ∈ Z. Since |2α| ≤ 2, we get 2α ∈ {−2,−1,0,1,2}, so α ∈ {0, ±1/2, ±1}. [My addition: these values are attained for n = 4, 6, 3, 1, 2, so the list is exactly n ∈ {1,2,3,4,6}.]

(2) A remark on lecture notes: the method of transforming the divergence by Gauss's integral theorem (Kollegheft Potentialtheorie 2, SS 1902, p. 37) also works in arbitrary oblique (non-orthogonal) curvilinear coordinates. [My reading of the method: one computes ∫ div v dV = ∮ v·n dS over an infinitesimal coordinate cell. In modern form this gives div v = (1/√g) ∂_i(√g v^i), where g = det(g_ij). That formula holds for any curvilinear coordinates, not just orthogonal (Lamé) ones.]

(3) Recovering a continuous f from its iterated integrals.
- The data are I_1 = ∫_0^1 f dx, I_2 = ∫_0^1∫_0^x f, I_3 = ∫_0^1∫_0^x∫_0^x f, and so on.
- Discretize: f_i = f(i/n).
- First equation: Σ_{i=1}^n f_i/n = I_1.
- Second equation: the inner integral is approximated by right Riemann sums, ∫_0^{j/n} f ≈ Σ_{i≤j} f_i/n. Summing over j gives Σ_j Σ_{i≤j} f_i/n² = Σ_i (n−i+1) f_i/n² = I_2. These are exactly Hilbert's coefficients n, n−1, n−2, …, 1 over n².
- In general [my addition]: I_k = ∫_0^1 (1−t)^{k−1}/(k−1)! f(t) dt (Cauchy's formula for repeated integration). The discrete analogue has coefficients C(n−i+k−1, k−1)/n^k.
- Hilbert proposes solving these n linear equations for f_1, …, f_n. Better, he says, determine ∫_0^1 w(x) f(x) dx ≈ Σ w_i f_i for an arbitrary weight w directly as a linear combination of the I_k.
- In modern terms: the I_k are the moments of f against powers of (1−t). The problem is moment inversion: express a linear functional of f through its moments, which amounts to approximating w by polynomials.

(4) Question on the foundations of measure. Can the theory of area and volume, for regions with arbitrary curved boundary, be founded on Cavalieri's principle alone? In the plane the principle must be stated thus: all figures lying between the same two parallels have equal area if every parallel line cuts out segments of equal length in their interiors.
errors: Item 3: the coefficient of f_3 in the second equation is written as (n−2)f_3/n. It should be (n−2)f_3/n² to match the other terms; this is a slip.

Item 3: the convergence is not justified. The discretized equations hold only approximately (with O(1/n) errors). The resulting linear system is a Pascal/Vandermonde-type moment system and is severely ill-conditioned. Solving it exactly need not give values f_i close to f(i/n) as n→∞. This presumably motivates Hilbert's switch to estimating ∫ w f directly. Even so, uniqueness and recovery need the Weierstrass approximation theorem or a moment-problem argument, which the note does not supply.
Item 1 is correct. 'ganze Zahl' must be read as 'algebraic integer'. The step 'rational algebraic integer ⇒ rational integer' is used implicitly.

results.what: cos(2π/n) is rational only for the values 0, ±1/2, ±1, proved via algebraic integers (ζ + ζ^{-1} is a rational algebraic integer).
results.modern_name: Rational values of cosine at rational multiples of π (cosine form of Niven's theorem)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical folklore. Published, e.g., by D.H. Lehmer (1933) and I. Niven (1956, Irrational Numbers); the same algebraic-integer argument is standard.

results.what: Deriving the divergence via Gauss's theorem works in arbitrary non-orthogonal curvilinear coordinates.
results.modern_name: Divergence in general curvilinear coordinates, div v = (1/√g) ∂_i(√g v^i)
results.usually_credited_to: Lamé (orthogonal case); Ricci-Curbastro and Levi-Civita (1900, general tensor form); also Beltrami.

results.what: Determining f, or ∫ w f, from its iterated integrals (moments against (1−t)^k) by discretization and solving a linear system.
results.modern_name: Hausdorff moment problem / moment inversion; Cauchy repeated-integration formula; quadrature from moments
results.usually_credited_to: Stieltjes (1894), Hausdorff (1921) for the moment problem; Cauchy for the repeated-integration formula.

results.what: Question whether Cavalieri's principle alone can serve as the foundation of area/volume theory for curved regions, with a precise formulation of the planar principle.
results.modern_name: Cavalieri's principle as an axiom of measure theory (cf. Fubini; Hilbert's third problem; Jordan/Lebesgue measure)
results.usually_credited_to: Cavalieri (1635). Axiomatic studies of area and volume by Hilbert (Grundlagen 1899), Dehn (1900), Lebesgue (1902).

deep.surprise_reason: Item 1 is a textbook application of algebraic integers, natural for Hilbert. Item 2 is a remark on his own lecture notes. Item 3 is a heuristic, unfinished sketch of moment inversion. Item 4 is a foundational question in line with his known interest in area and volume (Grundlagen, the third problem). Nothing here anticipates a later result in a significant way.

checkable.asserts: The listed rational values occur for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6.
2cos(2π/5) is an irrational algebraic integer, illustrating the argument (rational only if the minimal polynomial has degree 1).
Cauchy formula: ∫_0^1∫_0^x f = ∫_0^1 (1−t) f(t) dt, checked for one sample f.
Hilbert's second discretized sum, with weights (n−i+1)/n², converges to ∫_0^1∫_0^x f (here f = t², giving 1/12).
The general formula div v = (1/√g) ∂_i(√g v^i) in polar coordinates (with contravariant components) reduces to the known expression.

transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'also α =' reads in the image as 'also nur α = 0, ±1/2, ±1'. 'nur' is inserted above the line, and the transcription marks it as an insertion.
Second equation, third term: the image shows '(n−2) f_3/n'. This is a slip by Hilbert (should be n²), not a transcription error; leave as is but flag it.
'mit Hülfe der Gaussischen Integralsatzes' should grammatically be 'des Gaussischen Integralsatzes'. The handwriting is ambiguous; the struck word after it is illegible.
'ist eine ganze Zahl' in line 2 means an algebraic integer ('ganze algebraische Zahl'); the transcription is fine as written.
The leading struck symbol before 'ist eine ganze Zahl' is a deleted fragment; '= e^{2πi/n}' is written above it as an insertion.
